weight_summary.finding: Of thirteen steps, two are theorems (T2, and T4 conditional on T5's choices). The weight neither concentrates on one postulate nor rests on well-established steps: it is spread across eight non-theorem steps (T5, T6, T8, T9, T10, T11, T12, T13), each individually sufficient to break the conclusion, none of them well established. position_a.claim: Under a one-parameter family of metrics in which the perturbation is small but its first derivatives need not be small, the effective stress-energy of small-scale inhomogeneity is traceless (Theorem 1, Eq. 7) and satisfies the weak energy condition (Theorem 2, Eq. 8), so it 'must be of the form of a P=rho/3 fluid, and therefore cannot mimic dark energy'. Separately, apparent acceleration obtained from Buchert averaging of a poorly approximated metric is 'entirely spurious' and 'not a physical effect'.
position_a.key_assumption: Assumption (iv): local averages of quadratic products of the first derivatives of the metric perturbation have a weak limit (Eq. 5), together with (ii) |gamma_ab| <= lambda C_1(x) and (iii) |grad_c gamma_ab| <= C_2(x). They also restrict to k = 0 (Sec. 4.1) and make no claim that average spatial curvature must stay near FLRW.

position_b.claim: The trace-free theorem 'fails to be a mathematically general statement'; a weak-energy-condition result 'would be fine but irrelevant for backreaction'; and in the two-dimensional analogy the curvature-averaging assumption 'assumes what is to be proven'.
position_b.key_assumption: That assumption (iv) excludes the physically relevant regime: 'The condition (iv) is not motivated by any transparent and natural physical argument' (Sec. 3.4), because it requires perturbations down to arbitrarily small wavelengths whereas 'real perturbations do not continue to zero wavelength' (Sec. 4.2).

objections.turns_on: Which idealisation applies to the real universe, not mathematics. Neither side alleges a mathematical error: Green & Wald record that 'all assertions that we made mathematical errors in our work have been removed' from the revision (arXiv:1506.06452, Introduction), and their only factual concession is narrow. Both sides also agree the Buchert system is underdetermined. Decisively, Green & Wald themselves disclaim the strong reading: 'whether, in our actual universe, there might be significant backreaction' is not addressed by their analysis, and the closeness of the metric to FLRW 'does not imply that backreaction effects of inhomogeneities must be negligible' (arXiv:1407.8084, Sec. 2). On the other side Buchert and Rasanen concede the magnitude is not established: 'the effect has not been quantified in a fully realistic model' (arXiv:1112.5335, Sec. 5), and 'At the moment it is not yet clear whether backreaction is quantitatively important or not' (arXiv:1102.0408, Sec. 1.1). TWO FURTHER CORRECTIONS: (1) Green & Wald's theorems concern Q-type backreaction and therefore do not engage timescape, whose Omega-bar_Q0 = -0.0293; the argument that does reach it is their Sec. 3 spurious-curvature claim, which has no published reply addressed to timescape. (2) Green & Wald do not mention timescape or Wiltshire anywhere; they critique Buchert by name. Treating this dispute as timescape's decisive battleground, as the seed does, is a category error.
objections.third_party_adjudication: None found. The only candidate, arXiv:1512.02947 (Ostrowski & Roukema, MG14 proceedings), is by a co-author of arXiv:1505.07800. Green & Wald's reply (arXiv:1506.06452) was never published in a journal and has no DOI, while the Buchert et al. side appeared in CQG, so the exchange never closed in the refereed literature.

The record contains the proponent's own gauge concessions plus one dismissive sentence from Rasanen with no calculation. objections.independence_from_O1: O1 and O2 are independent in both directions, and timescape's own numbers make this sharper than the seed does. Granting O1 entirely in backreaction's favour does not establish the clock-rate postulate, which is an addition to GR. Granting O2 entirely in Wiltshire's favour does not require winning O1 - and more than that, timescape does not need a large Q at all: Omega-bar_Q0 = -0.0293, |Omega-bar_Q| <~ 0.042 always, q-bar > 0, backreaction '<5%' of the energy density. A resolution of O1 against large backreaction would refute the Buchert-acceleration programme that timescape is usually grouped with, not timescape itself. What timescape needs from the averaging literature is large average negative spatial curvature, and the only retrieved argument against that is Green & Wald Sec. 3.

position_a.claim: Inherited standardisation is a route to circularity, so the LCDM-derived corrections must be discarded: Pantheon+ bias corrections 'are not accounted for, as they introduce a bias towards the standard cosmology based on the FLRW metric', and Scolnic et al.'s alpha and beta are rejected because they were fitted in wCDM.
position_a.key_assumption: That discarding the corrections leaves a less biased dataset than keeping them.

position_b.claim: The bias corrections depend only weakly on the input cosmology: 'the sensitivity of the bias corrections to the input cosmology is relatively weak ... We therefore do not include this as an additional systematic'; and the nuisance-parameter minimisation is 'a cosmology-independent minimization'. DES validates this with 25 realisations analysed under six reference cosmologies, recovering the true distance-redshift relation to within 1 sigma 'even given a reference cosmology that is ~10 sigma from the truth'.
position_b.key_assumption: That the weak dependence demonstrated across FLRW reference cosmologies extends to a non-FLRW expansion history. DES states the risk explicitly: 'The bias correction step thus holds the biggest potential for harbouring cosmological assumptions that could influence the cosmological results'.

objections.turns_on: Whether a bias correction validated across FLRW reference cosmologies is valid against a non-FLRW expansion history. Both camps agree the step is where cosmological assumptions could bite; they disagree about whether the demonstrated insensitivity transfers. THE CHECKABLE FINDING: the timescape analyses avoid inheriting an LCDM calibration and thereby inherit uncorrected selection bias instead - 'Without the standard corrections, biases such as the Malmquist bias are present in our analysis'. DES avoids selection bias and inherits a flat-LCDM reference cosmology validated only within FLRW. NO PUBLISHED ANALYSIS DOES BOTH. Every Bayes factor in the ledger is conditional on which bias one chooses to carry.

rivals.name: Buchert averaging with backreaction, WITHOUT the clock-effect postulate (the priority comparison)
rivals.mechanism: Scalar averaging with a closure - either exact scaling solutions with dynamical spatial curvature, or a smoothed template metric with time-evolving constant spatial curvature - and no wall/void lapse.
rivals.differs_from_timescape_in: It drops T9-T11 and therefore REQUIRES genuine volume acceleration, which timescape does not have (q-bar > 0). Larena et al. state it: the model works 'without requiring an additional Dark Energy component', '(though a volume acceleration is still needed)', and 'a high level of backreaction is needed and acceleration of the effective scale factor still occurs'.
rivals.constraint_status: ANSWERED, in three forms. (1) At matched parameter count on the same supernovae, dropping the clock effect costs nothing: AIC at z_min = 0.033 is -228 for flat LCDM (9 params), -227 for timescape (9), -227 for the scaling solution with n = -1 (9), -225 for n free (10), and the authors state 'the scaling solution with n=-1 and the timescape model overall have the highest AIC likelihoods'. CAVEAT: confirm the AIC sign convention from the paper before quoting a direction. (2) An independent fit to SNLS plus WMAP3 peak positions gives 'The difference in the chi^2 between the two models is 3.9' against flat FLRW with quintessence, best fit Omega_m^D0 = 0.38, n = 0.12, H_D0 = 78.54 km/s/Mpc, Omega_b h^2 = 0.0255 - but NO absolute chi-squared, no error bars and no tables are published, so the statistic is UNINTERPRETABLE under ledger rule C6, and the authors say 'it is consistent with current data, but the constraints are not very strong'. (3) The required backreaction is not achievable on the best realistic estimates: Rasanen's peak model gives |Omega_Q| 'below 0.04 in absolute value' against '|Omega_Q| >~ 0.2 is needed', short by about a factor of five, with the expansion rate rising 'on a timescale of 10-100 billion years' and 'the increase is not rapid enough to correspond to acceleration'; the semi-realistic model achieves '15-25%' in H_D t against 20-70% needed, with 'just less deceleration' and 'The model cannot be trusted beyond an order of magnitude'. The strong-backreaction option requires Omega_m^D0 ~ 3%, reinterpreted as 'kinematical Dark Matter'. SO: what the clock effect buys is not a better supernova fit but the ability to avoid needing volume acceleration - it relocates the required large quantity from Q, where realistic estimates fall short by ~5x, to <R>, where no comparable realistic estimate exists. CLEAN NEGATIVE: no paper performs an ablation, fitting the same supernova dataset with and without the clock-rate postulate.

rivals.name: Swiss-cheese and perturbative backreaction models
rivals.mechanism: Exact LTB holes glued into an FLRW background (Swiss cheese), or second-order perturbation theory on an FLRW background.
rivals.differs_from_timescape_in: Both impose FLRW matching or perturbative smallness by construction, which timescape does not.
rivals.constraint_status: Small effects, and the smallness is substantially a construction consequence BY THE AUTHORS' OWN ACCOUNTS - but not in the way the seed implies. Marra, Kolb & Matarrese: the light-cone averaged density ratio 'decreases by 17%' while the expansion rate is unaffected, best fit w ~= 0; the FLRW matching is explicit in the construction but they do NOT draw the inference that it forces the effect to be small. Vanderveld, Flanagan & Wasserman: Monte Carlo over 10,000 realisations of five void passages gives a mean distance-modulus shift of -0.003 mag with standard deviation 0.11 mag, and 'this particular model cannot explain the supernova data'; they attribute the smallness to weak-field lensing and mass compensation, 'true within the domain of validity of weak lensing theory', NOT to FLRW matching. Clarkson, Ananda & Larena: about 10^-5 for the concordance model averaged on Hubble scales, 'as expected in perturbation theory' - an expectation of the second-order construction; they also note backreaction 'cannot be said to vanish on very large scales'. So none of these bounds a non-perturbative, non-mass-compensated scheme, which is exactly the regime Buchert et al. say the Green-Wald conditions exclude. That connects O5 to O1.

seed_corrections.was: 'what does backreaction alone achieve without D6, quantitatively? This single comparison is worth more than any other in this document.'
seed_corrections.should_be: ANSWERED in three forms. At matched parameter count on the same supernovae, dropping the clock effect costs nothing (Desgrange, Heinesen & Buchert: AIC -227 for both the n = -1 scaling solution and timescape, 9 parameters each). An independent fit exists (Larena et al.: Delta chi^2 = 3.9, but no absolute chi-squared, so uninterpretable) and it explicitly requires genuine volume acceleration, which timescape does not have. And the required backreaction is not achievable on the best realistic estimates (Rasanen: |Omega_Q| < 0.04 against >~ 0.2 needed; 15-25% in H_D t against 20-70%; 'just less deceleration'). So the clock effect buys the ability to avoid needing volume acceleration, relocating the required large quantity from Q to <R>. No ablation study exists.

seed_corrections.was: 'whether the smallness is a result or a consequence of the construction'
seed_corrections.should_be: It differs by paper and none matches the implied FLRW-matching story. Perturbative smallness is 'as expected in perturbation theory'; Swiss-cheese smallness follows from weak-field lensing and mass compensation, 'true within the domain of validity of weak lensing theory'; and Marra et al. do not draw the FLRW-matching inference at all. None of these bounds a non-perturbative, non-mass-compensated scheme, which connects this entry to O1.

seed_corrections.should_be: No. His own numbers fall short by about a factor of five on Omega_Q, and he dismisses the clock mechanism in one sentence with no calculation. The only timescape mention in the review he co-wrote is neutral and does not mention the clock effect.
